original_question: Can both cystic fibrosis (CF) and campomelic dysplasia (CMD) be classified as genetic disorders?

final_qi.question: Is cystic fibrosis classified as a genetic disorder?
final_qi.long_answer: Cystic fibrosis is universally recognized as a genetic disorder. It is caused by pathogenic variants in the CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene located on chromosome 7. Inheritance follows an autosomal-recessive pattern: an affected individual receives two defective CFTR alleles, one from each parent. The defective protein alters chloride and bicarbonate transport across epithelial cell membranes, leading to the characteristic multisystem manifestations (viscous airway secretions, recurrent pulmonary infections, pancreatic insufficiency, elevated sweat chloride, etc.). Because its etiology is rooted in inherited gene mutations and not in environmental or acquired factors, all major medical and genetic authorities (e.g., NIH, WHO, GeneReviews) classify cystic fibrosis as a genetic disorder.

final_qi.question: Is campomelic dysplasia classified as a genetic disorder?
final_qi.long_answer: Campomelic dysplasia is a well-characterised skeletal dysplasia caused by pathogenic variants in the SOX9 gene or chromosomal rearrangements that disrupt SOX9 regulation. Although most cases arise de novo, the condition results directly from an identifiable genetic alteration and is therefore classified as a genetic disorder (autosomal-dominant in terms of inheritance pattern when it is transmitted).

Cystic fibrosis is caused by pathogenic variants in the CFTR gene and is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, while campomelic dysplasia results from mutations in the SOX9 gene or related chromosomal rearrangements and follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern when transmitted. Thus, both conditions are rooted in genetic alterations.
